paras: The assault on W. L. Taylor was a beating of a Washington, D.C., attorney by a group of white men, described as "white ruffians," in the summer of 1910. Taylor survived, and by mid-August he was able to go out again. The attack is known only from short notices of his recovery in two of the city's Black weeklies.

According to the Washington Bee, Attorney W. L. Taylor, of 609 F street northwest, "was brutally assaulted by white ruffians a few weeks ago," which places the attack in about July 1910. The National Forum described the attackers as "a gang of white ruthens [ruffians]" and dated the attack only to "some time ago." Neither paper said where the assault took place, how it began, how many men were involved or whether any of them were known.

On August 13 the Bee reported that Taylor was "able to be out again, but not thoroughly well." A week later the National Forum said he was out again "and is doing nicely." No report of an arrest, charge or trial appears in the coverage.

Both reports ran as single sentences in local society columns, between notices of vacations, illnesses and visitors, rather than as news stories. The Bee's item sat among items about other Washington attorneys and physicians, and the Forum's among notes on local businessmen and social events. Both papers called the assault brutal and named the attackers' race, but neither commented further. No white-press account of the attack appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Assault on W. L. Taylor
bases: Both notices say the attorney was 'brutally assaulted' by 'white ruffians' or 'a gang' of them, a group beating with no killing or threat to kill reported (A1, A2).

Two different Washington Black weeklies, in independently worded local notices a week apart, agree that Attorney Taylor was brutally assaulted by white ruffians and was recovering (A1, A2); neither describes the attack itself.
